questions.text: During which months does the Amihan (Northeast Monsoon) prevail in the Philippines, and from which cardinal direction does it blow?

options.text: October to March from the northeast, bringing cool, dry air suitable for natural ventilation
June to September from the southwest, bringing warm moisture-laden air and heavy rainfall
April to May from the southeast, representing the hottest and most variable wind season
December to February from the northwest, coinciding with the coldest period in northern Luzon

rationale.summary: Amihan = Northeast monsoon, October to March, bringing cool dry air from the northeast — the desirable breeze for natural ventilation.
rationale.explanation: The Amihan is the Northeast Monsoon prevailing from approximately October to March (the dry season). It brings cool, dry winds from the northeast direction and is the desirable wind for natural ventilation in Philippine buildings. Primary living and working spaces, along with operable windows, should be oriented to capture Amihan breezes. Option A describes the Habagat (SW monsoon, June–September). Options C and D are fabricated distractors. The most common ALE error is reversing the months and directions of Amihan and Habagat.
common_misconceptions: Reversing the Amihan and Habagat — confusing NE/Oct–Mar with SW/Jun–Sep
Associating the desirable ventilation wind with the wet season rather than the dry season

questions.explanation: Amihan = NE monsoon = Oct–Mar = cool/dry = desirable for ventilation. This is the single most tested monsoon fact on the LEA.

questions.text: For a building in Manila during the transition months of April and May, which passive cooling strategy is most critical, and why?

options.text: Opening all northwest-facing windows to capture the consistent northwest monsoon breeze during April and May, which is not typical for this period
Deploying horizontal overhangs on the south facade, because December solar patterns extend into April and May, affecting solar heat gain
Maximizing mechanical HVAC capacity, since April–May are the hottest months when passive cooling is least effective due to hot, dry, variable winds
Maximizing cross-ventilation from the southwest because the Habagat begins in April and provides the coolest breezes, which is not accurate for this time

rationale.summary: April–May are the hottest, driest months with highly variable winds — passive cooling is least effective; these months drive peak HVAC load design.
rationale.explanation: The article identifies April–May as transition months: hot, dry, and with highly variable winds. These are the hottest months of the year and the period when passive cooling strategies are least effective, making them the critical driver of HVAC peak load design. No consistent monsoon (Amihan or Habagat) is blowing during this period, so there is no reliable Amihan breeze to capture (A is wrong). South overhangs are most critical in December (C is wrong). The Habagat does not begin until approximately June (D is wrong and reverses Habagat characteristics).
common_misconceptions: Assuming that passive strategies always suffice in the Philippines regardless of season
Confusing the April–May transition period with the onset of the Habagat season

questions.explanation: April–May is the Philippine hottest period with variable winds — passive cooling is least effective, and these months set the HVAC peak load design condition.

questions.text: What is the approximate solar noon altitude angle in Manila (latitude 14.6°N) at the June solstice (solar declination δ = +23.45°), and what design implication does this create?

options.text: Approximately 52°; horizontal overhangs on the south facade are most critical at this time, providing necessary shading
Approximately 66°; the sun is in the north of the building and no south-facade shading is needed, reducing the need for overhangs
Approximately 38°; the sun is low in the sky and vertical fins are required on all facades to manage glare and heat
Approximately 81°; the sun is nearly overhead, making horizontal overhangs less effective and roof insulation more important

rationale.summary: α_noon = 90° − |14.6° − 23.45°| = 90° − 8.85° = 81.15°. The sun is nearly directly overhead; horizontal overhangs are less effective at this high angle.
rationale.explanation: At Manila (φ = 14.6°N) at the June solstice (δ = +23.45°): α_noon = 90° − |φ − δ| = 90° − |14.6° − 23.45°| = 90° − 8.85° = 81.15°. With the sun almost directly overhead, horizontal overhangs provide minimal shading benefit. Roof insulation and ventilation become critical. Additionally, the sun can briefly appear on the north side of the building near the June solstice — a Philippine-specific nuance (Trap 3) that differs from temperate-zone design rules. Option A (52°) is the December solstice value. Option C (38°) is incorrect. Option D overstates the northward lean.
common_misconceptions: Applying the December solstice altitude (52°) to June, and vice versa
Assuming the sun never reaches the north side of a Philippine building, as it would in temperate climates

questions.explanation: At the June solstice in Manila, the sun is ~81° above the horizon at noon — nearly overhead — making roof insulation and ventilation, not south overhangs, the priority.

questions.text: During which months does the Habagat (Southwest Monsoon) prevail, and what design measure does it specifically require for southwest-facing facades?

options.text: October to March; orient operable windows to face southwest for maximum cross-ventilation, which is not advisable during the Habagat due to heavy rains
June to September; protect southwest facades with extended overhangs of at least 600 mm, rain screens, and minimal openings
April to May; install vertical fins on the southwest facade to deflect the wind-driven rain, which is not typical for this period
June to September; maximize southwest-facing glazing to capture the moisture-laden breezes for passive cooling, which contradicts the need for protection from rain

rationale.summary: Habagat = SW monsoon, June–September. SW facades require extended overhangs (≥600 mm), rain screens, and minimal operable openings to manage driving rain.
rationale.explanation: The Habagat prevails from approximately June to September, bringing warm, moisture-laden winds from the southwest that carry heavy rains and typhoon-associated weather. Southwest-facing facades must be protected with extended overhangs of at least 600 mm, rain screens, and minimal operable openings — waterproofing and drainage performance are most critical during Habagat. Option A confuses Habagat months with Amihan months. Option C uses the correct months but cites vertical fins, which are for solar shading, not rain protection. Option D would increase water ingress rather than prevent it.
common_misconceptions: Confusing Habagat (June–Sep, SW) with Amihan (Oct–Mar, NE)
Treating the SW monsoon wind as a ventilation resource rather than a rain protection challenge

questions.explanation: Habagat = SW monsoon = Jun–Sep = driving rain = protect, not ventilate. Extended overhangs ≥600 mm are the primary protective response.

questions.text: Which building facade in the Philippines receives the most intense heat gain and requires vertical shading devices (fins or louvers) rather than horizontal overhangs?

options.text: North facade, which receives the most solar radiation because the Philippines is south of the Tropic of Cancer
South facade, which consistently receives the highest sun angle and the most intense daily heat gain
East facade, which receives low-angle morning sun and accumulates the most heat before noon
West facade, which receives low-angle afternoon sun from 1:00–5:00 PM creating the most intense heat gain

rationale.summary: The west facade receives low-angle afternoon sun (1:00–5:00 PM) producing the most intense heat gain; vertical fins or louvers are required because horizontal overhangs cannot block low-angle sun.
rationale.explanation: The west facade receives low-angle afternoon sun from approximately 1:00–5:00 PM year-round, creating the most intense heat gain of any orientation. Because the sun angle is low (near the horizon), horizontal overhangs are ineffective — vertical fins, louvers, or deep wall recesses are required. The south facade (B) has a higher sun angle and can be effectively shaded with horizontal devices. The north facade (A) receives minimal direct sun year-round. The east facade (C) also receives low-angle sun but in the cooler morning hours, making it less critical. This is documented Trap 2 in the article.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the south facade is worst for heat gain because that applies in temperate-zone design rules
Believing horizontal overhangs can shade low-angle east and west sun the same way they shade high-angle south sun

questions.explanation: West = worst heat gain in the Philippines due to low-angle afternoon sun; vertical shading devices are essential because horizontal overhangs alone are insufficient.

questions.text: An architect in Manila is designing horizontal overhangs for a south-facing window that is 1.8 m tall. At the December solstice, the solar noon altitude angle is approximately 52°. Using D = H / tan(α), what is the minimum required overhang depth?

options.text: 0.94 m, resulting from incorrectly dividing the window height by tan(38°) rather than tan(52°)
1.80 m, which simply uses the window height as the overhang depth without applying the formula
2.30 m, which overestimates by applying the complementary angle (38°) in the numerator

rationale.explanation: The overhang depth formula is D = H / tan(α), where H is the window height (1.8 m) and α is the solar altitude angle at the critical design time. tan(52°) ≈ 1.28. D = 1.8 / 1.28 = 1.406 ≈ 1.41 m. The December solstice is the critical design condition for south-facade shading in Manila because the sun is at its lowest noon angle (most southerly position), requiring the deepest overhang. Option A uses tan(38°) = 0.78, giving 1.8 / 0.78 = 2.31 m — overcalculated. Option C simply equates depth to window height. Option D is an overestimate.
common_misconceptions: Using the complementary angle (90° − α) in the formula instead of the solar altitude angle α
Equating the overhang depth to the window height without applying the trigonometric formula

questions.explanation: D = H / tan(α) is the standard overhang depth formula; the December solstice noon altitude (~52° for Manila) is the critical south-facade design condition.

questions.text: Under PD 1096, Rule VIII, what is the minimum percentage of floor area that windows must provide for natural light, and what percentage of the floor area must the openable portion provide for ventilation?

options.text: Minimum 10% of floor area for natural light; minimum 5% of floor area for the openable ventilation portion
Minimum 5% of floor area for natural light; minimum 10% of floor area for the openable ventilation portion
Minimum 15% of floor area for natural light; minimum 7.5% of floor area for the openable ventilation portion
Minimum 8% of floor area for natural light; minimum 4% of floor area for the openable ventilation portion

rationale.summary: PD 1096 Rule VIII requires windows of at least 10% of floor area for natural light; the openable portion must be at least 5% of floor area for ventilation.
rationale.explanation: PD 1096, Rule VIII specifies that windows must provide a minimum of 10% of the floor area for natural light, and the openable (operable) portion of those windows must constitute a minimum of 5% of the floor area for natural ventilation. These requirements inform the cross-ventilation strategy and directly affect passive cooling performance. Option A reverses the light and ventilation percentages. Options C and D present values not found in PD 1096 Rule VIII.
common_misconceptions: Reversing the 10% (light) and 5% (ventilation) requirements from PD 1096 Rule VIII
Assuming both light and ventilation require the same percentage of floor area

questions.explanation: PD 1096 Rule VIII: 10% of floor area for light, 5% openable for ventilation — a direct recall pair often tested in reverse order on the LEA.

questions.text: An architect estimates cross-ventilation airflow using the simplified formula Q = Cv × A × V. For an inlet window area of 2.0 m² with perpendicular Amihan wind at 3.0 m/s and Cv = 0.55, what is the estimated airflow rate?

options.text: 6.00 m³/s, calculated by multiplying Cv by A by V and doubling for the outlet opening
3.30 m³/s, calculated as 0.55 × 2.0 × 3.0 using the inlet opening area
1.65 m³/s, calculated by using a diagonal wind coefficient of 0.275 instead of the perpendicular value
0.37 m³/s, calculated by applying a significantly reduced urban wind speed instead of the Amihan reference value

rationale.summary: Q = Cv × A × V = 0.55 × 2.0 × 3.0 = 3.30 m³/s using the smaller of inlet or outlet openings.
rationale.explanation: The simplified natural ventilation formula is Q = Cv × A × V, where Cv = effectiveness coefficient (0.5–0.6 for perpendicular wind; 0.25–0.35 for diagonal), A = area of the smaller inlet or outlet opening, and V = wind velocity. Q = 0.55 × 2.0 × 3.0 = 3.30 m³/s. Amihan in urban Metro Manila typically delivers 2–5 m/s. Option A incorrectly doubles for the outlet. Option C uses a diagonal coefficient (0.275) when the wind is perpendicular. Option D substitutes a reduced wind speed without basis.
common_misconceptions: Adding inlet and outlet areas instead of using the smaller of the two in the formula
Applying the diagonal wind coefficient (0.25–0.35) when wind is stated to be perpendicular

questions.explanation: Q = Cv × A × V uses the smaller opening area; the Cv value changes with wind angle — 0.5–0.6 perpendicular vs. 0.25–0.35 diagonal.

questions.text: For effective cross-ventilation in a Philippine building, PD 1096 light and ventilation standards and tropical design principles require openings on at least how many walls, and in what spatial relationship?

options.text: One wall only, with a single large opening to maximize inlet area and overall airflow velocity
Three walls minimum, with at least one opening on each of the north, south, and east facades
Two walls, on at least two opposite or adjacent walls to create an air pressure differential for airflow
Four walls, with equal openings on all facades to achieve omnidirectional ventilation regardless of wind direction

rationale.summary: Cross-ventilation requires openings on at least two opposite or adjacent walls to create the inlet-outlet pressure differential that drives air movement.
rationale.explanation: Effective cross-ventilation — which is both a PD 1096 standard and a fundamental tropical design principle — requires openings on at least two opposite or adjacent walls. This inlet-outlet arrangement creates a pressure differential: positive pressure at the windward inlet and negative pressure at the leeward outlet drives airflow through the occupied space. A single opening (A) only allows single-sided ventilation, which is far less effective. Three walls (B) and four walls (D) may further improve performance but are not the minimum requirement.
common_misconceptions: Assuming a large single opening provides cross-ventilation — it provides only single-sided ventilation
Requiring three or four walls of openings when two opposite or adjacent walls satisfy the standard

questions.explanation: Cross-ventilation requires openings on at least two opposite or adjacent walls — the pressure differential between windward and leeward sides drives the airflow.

questions.text: A designer applies a temperate-climate rule that the south facade always requires the most aggressive shading devices. Evaluate this assumption for a building in Manila (14.6°N latitude).

options.text: The assumption is correct because the south facade faces the equator and receives maximum solar radiation year-round at 14.6°N latitude
The assumption is irrelevant because in the Philippines all facades receive identical solar radiation throughout the year, which is not accurate.
The assumption is fully correct; at 14.6°N the south facade has the lowest sun angle of any facade and the most intense heat gain, which is a common misconception.
The assumption is partially correct: the south facade needs horizontal shading, but the west facade requires more intensive treatment due to low-angle afternoon sun

rationale.summary: The south facade needs horizontal shading (manageable high-angle sun), but the west facade demands more intensive vertical shading devices due to intense low-angle afternoon sun.
rationale.explanation: This question tests documented Trap 3 from the article. In Manila (14.6°N), the south facade does receive consistent solar radiation and needs horizontal shading devices (overhangs, brise-soleil). However, the west facade receives low-angle afternoon sun (1:00–5:00 PM) that is far more intense and harder to shade — requiring vertical fins, louvers, or deep recesses. Horizontal overhangs alone cannot block low-angle west sun. Additionally, near the June solstice, the sun briefly appears on the north side of the building — a nuance that does not exist in temperate climates. Option A and C both overstate the south facade's priority. Option D is false.
common_misconceptions: Applying temperate-climate south-worst rules directly to Philippine low-latitude buildings
Assuming horizontal overhangs handle all facade orientations equally regardless of sun angle

questions.explanation: At 14.6°N, west outranks south for heat gain intensity; temperate rules misapplied to the Philippines produce incorrect shading device choices.

questions.text: What is the approximate solar noon altitude angle in Manila (latitude 14.6°N) at the June solstice (solar declination δ = +23.45°), and what design implication does this create?

options.text: Approximately 52°; horizontal overhangs on the south facade are most critical at this time, which is a common design strategy for lower sun angles.
Approximately 66°; the sun is in the north of the building and no south-facade shading is needed, which is incorrect for this latitude and time of year.
Approximately 38°; the sun is low in the sky and vertical fins are required on all facades, which misrepresents the sun's position during the solstice.
Approximately 81°; the sun is nearly overhead, making horizontal overhangs less effective and roof insulation more important

rationale.summary: α_noon = 90° − |14.6° − 23.45°| = 90° − 8.85° = 81.15°. The sun is nearly directly overhead; horizontal overhangs are less effective at this high angle.
rationale.explanation: At Manila (φ = 14.6°N) at the June solstice (δ = +23.45°): α_noon = 90° − |φ − δ| = 90° − |14.6° − 23.45°| = 90° − 8.85° = 81.15°. With the sun almost directly overhead, horizontal overhangs provide minimal shading benefit. Roof insulation and ventilation become critical. Additionally, the sun can briefly appear on the north side of the building near the June solstice — a Philippine-specific nuance (Trap 3) that differs from temperate-zone design rules. Option A (52°) is the December solstice value. Option C (38°) is incorrect. Option D overstates the northward lean.
common_misconceptions: Applying the December solstice altitude (52°) to June, and vice versa
Assuming the sun never reaches the north side of a Philippine building, as it would in temperate climates

questions.explanation: At the June solstice in Manila, the sun is ~81° above the horizon at noon — nearly overhead — making roof insulation and ventilation, not south overhangs, the priority.
